The clerk's pen tapped once against the counter, and something in her posture eased from copyist to business. "Mistress Brenna Hallowell," she said. "Desk clerk, and the one who has to walk you through it, so mind the questions." She pulled a ledger toward her and opened it to a fresh page. "Alaric Red. Spell it for me—R-E-D like the color, I'll assume?" She didn't wait long before dipping her pen. "Registration works so. It costs two silver, once, and that's the whole fee—never again. You sign the roll, we take your measure on the stone, and you start at Novice rank. That's the Guild's standing, lowest rung, and it's what lets you take contracts off that board there." extra.display_text:
Brenna looked up from her copying when the slip came down on the counter. "Glimmerdeep, is it." She pulled the board's ledger toward her, found the line, and wrote his name beside the entry in a quick, practiced hand. "Academy contract, that one. They want the outer level clear—crystal beetles and mineral slimes, mostly, though the report's a season old, so mind it." She stamped the slip with the Guild's seal, pressed it flat, and held it out. "That's yours. Don't lose it; it's what I close the work against when you come back." She capped the stamp and gave him a look over the counter, the kind a woman gives someone she expects to see again in one piece or not at all. "Grotto's a half-day west of the city, past the quarry road—ask at the west gate and they'll point you. Beetles bite and the slimes eat leather, so mind your boots and your straps." The pen dipped back into the ink. "Come back with the level cleared and the desk pays out. Anything else, you know where I sit." The slip was stiff paper, the antler seal dark blue in its corner, the ink of the terms still sharp: *Clear the Outer Grottos of Glimmerdeep — 90 cp, posted for the Glassmere Academy of Magic.* Outside the hall's open door, Glassmere's morning traffic clattered along—a cart, a dog, someone shouting about a delivery. The west gate lay somewhere down the street, past whatever the day put in the way.

He left the track where the ground sloped, boots loose on the scree, and the hollow opened up between two slabs of fallen rock. The light grew with every step until it wasn't a glow anymore but a thing. It stood about hip-high, a shard of pale crystal jutting from a patch of grey moss, wide as his spread hand at the base and tapering to a rough point. Each pulse came from inside it, a slow swell of blue-white that lit the hollow and died away over the space of a breath. The shimmering air sat above it in a faint column, and up close he could feel why: warmth, dry and still, coming off the stone like heat off a hearthstone hours after the fire. The moss around the crystal's foot had gone yellow and brittle in a neat circle, cooked by that warmth. The crystal itself was not glass-smooth. Fine cracks laced its sides, and in one of them, wedged deep, sat the corroded brass corner of something man-made—a plate, or the edge of one, furred green with age. It had not grown there. Something had struck it, or it had struck something, hard enough to bite metal into it. The pulse came again, and this time, this close, there was a sound under it: a low tone, more felt in the teeth than heard, rising and fading with the light. Somewhere in the hillside around him, faint as a memory, the tone seemed to answer back from two places—one deeper, toward the grotto's dark cut in the rock, and one thinner, off to the north. Then it settled back into its slow, patient pulse, and the hollow was quiet again except for the wind moving over the scree.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
He left the track where the ground sloped, boots loose on the scree, and the hollow opened up between two slabs of fallen rock. The light grew with every step until it wasn't a glow anymore but a thing.

It stood about hip-high, a shard of pale crystal jutting from a patch of grey moss, wide as his spread hand at the base and tapering to a rough point. Each pulse came from inside it, a slow swell of blue-white that lit the hollow and died away over the space of a breath. The shimmering air sat above it in a faint column, and up close he could feel why: warmth, dry and still, coming off the stone like heat off a hearthstone hours after the fire. The moss around the crystal's foot had gone yellow and brittle in a neat circle, cooked by that warmth.

The crystal itself was not glass-smooth. Fine cracks laced its sides, and in one of them, wedged deep, sat the corroded brass corner of something man-made—a plate, or the edge of one, furred green with age. It had not grown there. Something had struck it, or it had struck something, hard enough to bite metal into it.

The pulse came again, and this time, this close, there was a sound under it: a low tone, more felt in the teeth than heard, rising and fading with the light. Somewhere in the hillside around him, faint as a memory, the tone seemed to answer back from two places—one deeper, toward the grotto's dark cut in the rock, and one thinner, off to the north.

Then it settled back into its slow, patient pulse, and the hollow was quiet again except for the wind moving over the scree.

Cold air breathed out of it, a steady current that smelled of wet stone and something faintly sweet, like overripe fruit. Just inside, daylight reached far enough to show the floor: gravel and broken shale, and a litter of thin, translucent husks cracked open like shed shells, dry underfoot. Beetle casings, by their shape—each one the size of a dinner plate, split down the back. A great many of them, drifts of them, all along where the light died. A side passage branched off to the right within the first thirty feet, its mouth low and dark. Ahead, the main tunnel ran on into black, sloping gently down, and from somewhere along it came a sound—a slow, wet scrape, then silence, then the scrape again, unhurried, like something dragging itself over gravel and stopping to feed. Outside, the quarry road lay quiet in the midday light. Inside, the dark held the cold and the sweetness and the scraping, and waited to see what came into it.

mes:
The ring of force went out of the staff again, and this time nothing came back through it.

The small one's fractured shell gave all at once, the facet plates caving inward with a sound like a dropped dish, and it dropped where it stood, legs folding under it. The middle one, flank torn and plate gone, took the wave broadside and went over backward, clawing at the gravel for one long moment before the clawing stopped. The big one held its feet longest, fractures webbed white across its shoulder plates, took the force full in the chest, and its legs simply quit—the shell tipped, rocked once on its domed back, and lay still.

Then the chamber was quiet. The quartz ribs glowed on, indifferent, and the sweet-and-vinegar air sat cold in his throat. His forearm throbbed with his pulse, wet through the sleeve; his hip burned where the bruise had gone sharp; his calf ached where the bite had landed and released. Blood had run warm down to his wrist and dried tacky there.

Four beetle-shells lay around him in the quartz-glow, charred and cracked, and the pale chitin plates that had split free of them sat among the gravel—eight of the things, broad as a man's palm, catching the light flat and cold. They went into the small pouch at his belt without his having to think about it, the way the pouch took things, and weighed nothing after.

Something in him had changed with the killing. He felt it as a settling, a steadiness that had not been there an hour ago—not strength returning, nothing healed, but more of him than there had been, as if the morning's mana-sense had widened by a finger's breadth on either side.

The gravel fall at the far wall stood undisturbed. The side passage back toward the mouth breathed its cold draft. On, into the chamber's deeper dark, the tunnel went where it went.

The grotto had its own quiet—not silent, exactly: a faint ringing in the quartz, like a wet glass finger circling a rim, so low he heard it more in his teeth than his ears. Once, far off toward the deeper part, something shifted—a slow grinding, mineral and patient—and was still again. He kept his staff across his knees and let the time run. The light in the ribs never dimmed or brightened. There was no way to mark the hours except by his own body, and his body kept count for him: the forearm's wet throb slowing, cooling, the flesh knitting tight and itching under the crusted sleeve; the hip's bright spike sinking to an ache, then to a stiffness he could shift against; the calf loosening until he could stretch the leg out straight without paying for it. Blood dried, flaked, itched. Mana settled back into him by degrees, a rising tide he felt as fullness behind the breastbone, cool and patient. By the end his body had put most of itself back together. He was not what he had been at the grotto mouth—something still short of whole, a thinness left in him—but the arm took his weight when he pressed it against the rock, and the leg held him when he rose. Daylight's edge had to be gone outside. The quartz chamber glowed on, unchanged, indifferent to hours. The gravel fall at the far wall. The side passage back toward the mouth, breathing its cold draft. And the tunnel, onward, into part of the level nobody had shown him yet. The four cracked shells still lay where they had fallen.

He let the lance go from where he stood, and the heat of it bent the air down the tunnel.

The flame struck the ooze's crown and went into it. For a heartbeat the mass lit from inside—a glow of ember-orange threaded through the drifting glints, beautiful, almost—then the fire found everything at once. The ooze did not scream and did not run. It slumped, the way a candle slumps in a hot room, its clear body clouding, browning, cracking into sheets that sloughed off the dissolved basin and steamed on the wet stone. Within moments it was only a spreading pool of cooling slurry, glints settling in it like grit in syrup, and a smell of scorched mineral and something faintly sweet.

The hollow's air came back cold. The vein-light pulsed on.

Two lumps of pale gel had survived the fire, sitting in the residue—soft, quartz-flecked, faintly warm still. They went into the belt pouch without ceremony, and the pouch took them as it took everything.

He felt the kill settle into him the way the beetles' had: that same widening, more of him than there had been. The lance-work had come cleaner off the staff this time, too—he could feel it, the shaping of the spell sitting easier in his grip, as if the wood had learned something along with him.

The way on ran past the dead thing's basin, the stone there etched glass-smooth and still wet. On the other side the tunnel took up again, gravel underfoot, angling downward toward a part of the level no one had shown him.
